name: Graphics & Math
description: Vectors, matrices, transforms, quaternions, the rendering pipeline and shader fundamentals.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What Graphics & Math is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is a vector, in graphics and games?
cards.answer: A quantity with a direction and a length, written as components such as (x, y) or (x, y, z). Vectors represent positions, movement directions, velocities and forces.
cards.explanation: Adding a velocity vector to a position vector each frame is how things move. The length of a vector (its magnitude) is found with Pythagoras: √(x² + y² + z²).

cards.prompt: How do coordinate systems work in graphics?
cards.answer: Every point has coordinates measured from an origin along axes: x and y in 2D, plus z in 3D. Screens usually put the origin at the top-left with y increasing downwards; 3D engines put it at the world centre with y (or z) pointing up.
cards.explanation: Different engines and tools disagree on which axis is "up" and on left- versus right-handed systems, a frequent source of flipped or mirrored models when importing assets.

cards.prompt: What is a transformation matrix used for?
cards.answer: A grid of numbers that encodes a transformation — moving (translation), rotating or scaling — so that multiplying a point by it applies the transformation. Several transformations combine into one matrix by multiplying them.
cards.explanation: GPUs are extremely fast at matrix maths, which is why every vertex of every model passes through a few matrix multiplications to reach its place on screen.

cards.prompt: What are pixels, resolution and RGB colour?
cards.answer: A pixel is one dot of the image grid; resolution is how many there are (1920 × 1080). Each pixel's colour is usually stored as red, green and blue intensities, commonly 0–255 each, plus optional alpha for transparency.
cards.explanation: Mixing light: (255, 0, 0) is pure red, (255, 255, 255) white and (0, 0, 0) black. A 1080p frame is about two million pixels, redrawn every frame.

cards.prompt: What does "rendering" mean?
cards.answer: Turning a description of a scene — models, materials, lights and a camera — into the 2D image shown on screen. Real-time rendering (games) must do it many times per second; offline rendering (films) can take minutes per frame.
cards.explanation: Real-time graphics mostly uses rasterisation (projecting triangles onto the pixel grid); ray tracing (simulating light rays) gives more realistic lighting and is increasingly used in games with hardware support.

modules.name: Vector & Matrix Math
modules.description: The linear algebra you use every day in graphics and games.

cards.prompt: What does the dot product tell you, and what is it used for?
cards.answer: `a · b = |a||b|cos θ`. With normalised vectors it is the cosine of the angle: 1 same direction, 0 perpendicular, −1 opposite. Used for lighting (surface normal vs light direction), field-of-view checks, and projecting one vector onto another.
cards.explanation: 'Is the enemy in front of me?' is `dot(forward, toEnemy) > 0`. Lambert diffuse lighting is `max(0, dot(N, L))`. Cheap and everywhere — one multiply-add per component.

cards.prompt: What does the cross product produce?
cards.answer: A vector perpendicular to both inputs, with magnitude `|a||b|sin θ` — the area of the parallelogram they span. Direction follows the right-hand rule (in a right-handed coordinate system).
cards.explanation: Used to compute surface normals from triangle edges, to build orthonormal bases, and to determine turn direction — the sign of the 2D cross product tells you whether a point is left or right of a line.

cards.prompt: Why does the object end up in the wrong place?
cards.code:
// intended: rotate the object, then move it 10 units right
mat4 model = rotate(radians(45.0)) * translate(vec3(10, 0, 0));
cards.answer: Matrix multiplication is not commutative and applies right-to-left: this translates first, then rotates that translation about the origin — swinging the object around. Write `translate * rotate` for rotate-then-move.
cards.explanation: The standard order for a model matrix is translate × rotate × scale, so scaling happens first and translation last. Getting this wrong produces objects that orbit the origin or shear when scaled — the classic first-week graphics bug.

cards.prompt: Why do games use quaternions instead of Euler angles for rotation?
cards.answer: Euler angles suffer gimbal lock — at certain orientations two axes align and a degree of freedom is lost — and they interpolate badly. Quaternions have no gimbal lock, compose cheaply, and interpolate smoothly with slerp.
cards.explanation: A unit quaternion encodes an axis and an angle in four numbers. Keep them normalised (floating-point drift accumulates), and remember q and −q represent the same rotation — which matters when interpolating, since slerp should take the short path.

cards.prompt: A vertex travels model → world → view → ___ → NDC → screen space.
cards.answer: clip
cards.explanation: Model matrix places the object in the world, view matrix moves the world into camera space, projection produces clip space, the perspective divide gives normalised device coordinates, and the viewport transform maps to pixels. Debugging a 'nothing renders' bug usually means finding which of these is wrong.

modules.name: Rendering & Shaders
modules.description: The pipeline, shader stages and what actually costs frame time.

cards.prompt: What are the stages of the rasterisation pipeline?
cards.answer: Vertex shader → (optional tessellation and geometry) → primitive assembly and clipping → rasterisation → fragment/pixel shader → per-fragment tests (depth, stencil, blending) → framebuffer.
cards.explanation: Vertex shaders run per vertex, fragment shaders per covered pixel — so a full-screen effect can run millions of fragment invocations. That asymmetry is why moving work from the fragment stage to the vertex stage, or to a lower resolution pass, is such a common optimisation.

cards.prompt: A scene with 5,000 small objects runs badly despite a low triangle count. Why?
cards.answer: Draw-call overhead: each one costs CPU work and a state change. Fix with batching, instancing for repeated meshes, texture atlases and shared materials so the renderer can group them.
cards.explanation: Modern GPUs eat triangles happily; the bottleneck is usually the CPU submitting work. Instancing draws thousands of copies with one call. Note that different materials break batching — which is why an atlas often outperforms 'cleaner' per-object textures.

cards.prompt: Vertex shader vs fragment shader
cards.answer: Vertex shaders transform vertices and output per-vertex data; fragment shaders compute the colour of each covered pixel using interpolated inputs.

left.title: Vertex
points: Outputs are interpolated across the triangle

right.title: Fragment
points: Runs per covered pixel — often millions
Branching can be costly on GPUs

cards.explanation: GPUs execute in lockstep groups (warps/wavefronts), so a branch taken by only some threads makes both paths execute. Prefer arithmetic and `mix`/`step` over conditionals in hot fragment code.

cards.prompt: Why does blending colours in sRGB produce muddy results?
cards.answer: sRGB values are gamma-encoded, not linear in light intensity. Averaging encoded values is not averaging light. Convert to linear space, do the maths, then convert back for display.
cards.explanation: This is why naive alpha blending and mipmaps can look wrong — dark fringes on transparent edges, grey halos. Modern engines work in linear space internally and apply the transfer function at the very end, along with tone mapping for HDR.

modules.name: Vectors, Matrices & Interpolation
modules.description: Normalisation, homogeneous coordinates, projection, handedness, lerp and easing.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
import math
v = (3.0, 4.0)
length = math.hypot(*v)
unit = tuple(round(x / length, 2) for x in v)
print(length)
print(unit)
print(round(math.hypot(*unit), 6))
cards.explanation: A vector's length (magnitude) is the square root of the sum of squared components — 3-4-5 here. Normalising divides by the length to get a unit vector: same direction, length 1. Directions for lighting, movement and dot-product tests should be normalised; normalising a zero vector divides by zero, so guard it.

cards.prompt: Why do graphics use 4×4 matrices and homogeneous coordinates for 3-D?
cards.answer: A 3×3 matrix can rotate and scale but cannot translate. Adding a fourth coordinate w lets translation be expressed as a matrix multiplication too, so any chain of translate, rotate, scale and projection collapses into one 4×4 matrix. Points use w = 1 (affected by translation); directions use w = 0 (not affected).
cards.explanation: The w component also makes perspective projection possible: the projection matrix puts depth into w, and dividing by w afterwards shrinks distant objects. Getting w wrong for normals or directions is a classic lighting bug.

cards.prompt: Perspective vs orthographic projection
cards.answer: Perspective projection makes distant objects smaller, converging towards vanishing points, like a real camera or eye; orthographic projection keeps sizes constant regardless of distance, with parallel lines staying parallel.

left.title: Perspective
points: Defined by field of view and aspect ratio
Depth precision concentrated near the camera

right.title: Orthographic
points: Defined by a box: left, right, top, bottom

cards.explanation: Perspective suits first- and third-person 3-D views; orthographic suits 2-D games, isometric views, UI, CAD and shadow-map rendering for directional lights. The near and far planes of a perspective projection affect depth precision — keep the near plane as far out as you can.

cards.prompt: Why do assets sometimes appear mirrored or face the wrong way between engines?
cards.answer: Engines disagree on coordinate conventions: right-handed (OpenGL, Blender, Godot) versus left-handed (Unity, Direct3D by convention, Unreal), and which axis points up (Y-up versus Z-up). Importing without converting flips geometry, reverses triangle winding (so faces are culled wrongly) and mixes up rotations.
cards.explanation: Exporters and importers convert these when configured correctly — always check the axis and handedness settings. The cross product's direction and rotation signs both depend on handedness, so maths copied between engines can silently flip.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.code:
def lerp(a, b, t):
    return a + (b - a) * t

print(lerp(10, 20, 0.5))
ease_in = lambda t: t * t
print([lerp(0.0, 1.0, ease_in(t)) for t in (0.0, 0.5, 1.0)])
cards.explanation: `lerp(a, b, t) = a + (b − a)·t` blends linearly between two values for t from 0 to 1. Easing functions reshape t before lerping — ease-in-quad (t²) starts slow and accelerates — to make motion feel natural. Slerp does the same on the sphere for rotations.

modules.name: Lighting, Textures & Techniques
modules.description: Lighting models and PBR, textures, UVs and mipmaps, normal mapping, depth buffers, shadows, anti-aliasing and ray tracing.

cards.prompt: How do the Phong/Blinn–Phong model and physically based rendering (PBR) differ?
cards.answer: Blinn–Phong sums ambient, diffuse (N·L) and specular highlight terms with artist-tuned constants — cheap and intuitive but not energy-conserving. PBR models surfaces with physical parameters (albedo, metallic, roughness) and microfacet BRDFs that conserve energy, so materials look right under any lighting.
cards.explanation: PBR is the standard in modern engines because one material works in every environment. Image-based lighting — environment maps for reflections and ambient light — is a large part of what makes PBR scenes convincing.

cards.prompt: What are UV coordinates and mipmaps?
cards.answer: UVs map each vertex to a position in a 2-D texture (0–1 range), and the rasteriser interpolates them across each triangle. Mipmaps are precomputed, progressively halved versions of a texture; the GPU samples the level matching the on-screen size.
cards.explanation: Without mipmaps, distant textures shimmer and alias because many texels fall inside one pixel, and cache use is poor. A full mip chain costs about one third more memory. Anisotropic filtering keeps textures sharp at glancing angles.

cards.prompt: What does a normal map do?
cards.answer: It stores per-pixel surface normals in a texture (RGB = XYZ, usually in tangent space), so lighting responds to fine detail — bricks, scratches, pores — on a low-polygon mesh without adding geometry.
cards.explanation: Normal maps change shading only, not silhouettes, so edges still look flat; displacement or parallax techniques add depth. The tangent basis must match between the baking tool and the engine, or lighting looks subtly wrong — the green channel convention (OpenGL versus DirectX) is a common mismatch.

cards.prompt: Two overlapping surfaces flicker as the camera moves. What is happening, and how do you fix it?
cards.answer: Z-fighting: the surfaces are at nearly the same depth, and the depth buffer lacks the precision to decide consistently which is in front. Separate the geometry, push the near plane further out (precision is concentrated near it), use a polygon offset for decals, or use a reversed-Z floating-point depth buffer.
cards.explanation: The depth buffer stores, per pixel, the depth of the nearest surface drawn so far; each fragment is kept only if it is nearer. With perspective projection its precision is non-linear, so a tiny near plane such as 0.001 wastes most of the precision close to the camera.

cards.prompt: How does shadow mapping work, and what are its typical artefacts?
cards.answer: First render the scene from the light's point of view, storing depths in a shadow map. Then, when shading each pixel from the camera, transform it into the light's space and compare its depth with the stored one: if something nearer to the light was recorded, the pixel is in shadow.
cards.explanation: Artefacts: shadow acne (self-shadowing stripes, fixed with a depth bias), peter-panning (shadows detached when the bias is too large), and jagged edges from limited resolution — addressed with cascaded shadow maps for large scenes and filtering (PCF) for soft edges.

cards.prompt: MSAA vs post-process anti-aliasing (FXAA) vs temporal anti-aliasing (TAA)
cards.answer: MSAA takes several coverage samples per pixel at geometry edges; FXAA blurs detected edges in a single post-process pass; TAA reuses jittered samples from previous frames, resolving detail over time.

left.title: MSAA / FXAA
points: MSAA: extra samples at triangle edges
MSAA: sharp, costly with deferred shading

cards.explanation: Deferred renderers make MSAA expensive, which is why TAA became the default in modern engines — and why upscalers (DLSS, FSR, XeSS) build on its temporal accumulation. TAA's cost is ghosting and softness in motion; FXAA is cheap but blurs texture detail.

cards.prompt: Rasterisation vs ray tracing
cards.answer: Rasterisation projects triangles onto the screen and shades the pixels they cover — extremely fast, but reflections, shadows and global illumination need approximations. Ray tracing follows rays from the camera into the scene, bouncing to other surfaces and lights, producing those effects physically.
cards.explanation: Hardware ray tracing made hybrid rendering practical: rasterise the primary view, then trace rays for reflections, shadows or global illumination, with denoisers cleaning up the few rays affordable per pixel. Film rendering path-traces everything offline.
